claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hybrid physics-informed machine-learning framework can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework couples a reduced-order physics-based model to a machine-learning regression algorithm.
A small, targeted set of tensile and fracture experiments is sufficient to calibrate the framework.
Machine-learning methods can predict Young’s modulus, yield-related properties, and toughness in alloys.

The framework is expected to remain reliable under standardized room-temperature tensile and mode-I fracture conditions with controlled strain rates when the hierarchical features remain statistically consistent.
Hierarchical heterogeneity and local chemical fluctuations mediate load transfer in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical heterogeneity and local chemical fluctuations mediate dislocation activity in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical heterogeneity and local chemical fluctuations mediate crack propagation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Physics-based constraints from reduced-order multiscale simulations narrow the machine-learning parameter space.
Focusing the model on physically meaningful microstructural descriptors enables rapid and reliable mapping from microscale physics to macroscopic mechanical responses.
The framework will predict each of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness to approximately ±10% of experimental measurements.
The framework will reduce computational cost by more than 50% relative to full-fidelity DFT/CALPHAD methods.
Exhaustive first-principles and related computational workflows are computationally expensive for alloy discovery.
Existing computational criteria are less effective at accurately predicting fracture toughness when relevant toughening mechanisms are not represented.
Unanticipated phase transformations or microstructural instabilities can cause the framework to lose reliability.
Processing-induced changes that move dominant microstructural features beyond the calibration domain can cause the framework to lose reliability.
Prediction accuracy and efficiency gains may vary with microstructural variability and limitations of the training dataset.
